title: Modular exporter chassis and adaptive flush sequencing
creator: Asha Patel
description: Replace monolithic exporter path with a modular 'chassis' that can load multiple lightweight exporter adapters at runtime and implement an adaptive flush/sequencing coordinator. Motivation: the current exporter implementation bundles large deps, creates head-of-line blocking on network/backpressure, and holds significant heap during spike bursts (OOM risk for small-footprint runtime). This ticket implements a pluggable exporter chassis + coordinator that does: 1) zero-allocation handoff for span batches where possible, 2) per-exporter backpressure tokens with soft/ hard limits, 3) adaptive flush sequencing (shorter flush windows under low-latency SLOs, aggregated flush at high-throughput tails), and 4) a compact fallback path that drops non-critical attributes when memory pressure is high.
proposed_solution: 1) Introduce exporter chassis interface (C ABI compatible) that supports adapter loading via config and health hooks. 2) Implement two reference adapters: async-multiplex-http (existing OTLP/HTTP optimized) and compact-file-sink for local edge nodes. 3) Build an adaptive flush coordinator that observes token latency, queue depth, and GC pause estimation to decide flush frequency and whether to compact attributes. 4) Replace the legacy sync exporter with a compatibility shim that delegates to the new chassis behind a feature flag (obs.modular_exporter_v2). 5) Add graceful shutdown sequencing: ordered drain of in-flight batches with timeout and fallback fast-path to persist partial payloads to disk for later forwarding. 6) Canary rollout via runtime flags + per-region rollout rules in Console. Note: keep schema compatibility for span envelopes and ensure headers required by downstream collectors continue to be sent.
acceptance_criteria: Feature flag obs.modular_exporter_v2 deployable to 10% of runtime fleet without error spikes
End-to-end latency for short traces (<=50 tokens) not worse than +5ms median compared to baseline in canary
99th-percentile exporter CPU reduced by >=20% in high-concurrency synthetic workload
Heap allocation during 5x burst traffic reduced by >=30% on a t4g-small runtime container
Graceful shutdown drains in-flight spans within configured timeout and persists partial payloads on forced stop
Backward-compatible span schema and headers verified against internal ingestion (ingest-team acceptance)
Automated unit and e2e tests covering backpressure paths and compacting behavior

risks:
- Exporter adapter API must remain stable across releases; mistaken ABI changes could break private deployments.
- The compacting heuristic may drop attributes that downstream jobs rely on for alerts; need careful default and opt-out.
- Backpressure tokens and adaptive sequencing add complexity that can mask upstream latency sources if observed only at exporter layer.
- Rolling back from canary requires a deterministic circuit-breaker and automatic failover to the legacy shim to avoid data loss.
testing_plan: Unit tests for chassis loading/unloading and adapter lifecycle
Load tests: 1k concurrent short requests and 10k long requests across 3 node sizes
Fault injection: target adapter returns 503s and high latency; verify backpressure and failover
Memory pressure: run GC stress tests and validate compaction thresholds trigger
Canary observability: compare export latency, token drops, and ingestion error rates between groups
End-to-end validation with ingestion team using sample production traces
notes: Benchmarks from prototype (local lab, 2026-02-20): async-multiplex-http reduced exporter CPU by ~28% at 2k RPS and reduced allocations by ~34% vs legacy; adaptive flush reduced tail latency variance in burst tests. Initial compaction policy: drop attributes with tag 'debug' and trim string attributes >1024 bytes. Feature flag name: obs.modular_exporter_v2. Canary plan: 10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100% with 24h observation windows and automatic rollback on >2x error rate regression. Timeline: prototype (2 weeks), integration + tests (3 weeks), canary (2 weeks).
